title: Kenyan Pili Pili Sauce
author: Mama Wanjiru

heritage.origin: National — present at every Kenyan table
heritage.history: Pili pili (the Swahili word for pepper/chilli) is the essential condiment of Kenyan cuisine. No nyama choma table, no roadside kiosk, and no proper Kenyan meal is complete without a small dish of pili pili sauce on the side. Every Kenyan family has their own recipe — some prefer fresh and sharp, others cooked and smoky, others with garlic and lemon. This is the foundational version.
heritage.modernEvolution: The blender and food processor have made pili pili faster to prepare, but many Kenyans still prefer the mortar and pestle for the more textured, rustic result it produces.

desc: Pili Pili is Kenya's essential hot sauce — blended fresh chillies, tomatoes, garlic, onion, and lemon juice into a fiery, fragrant condiment that belongs on every Kenyan table. No nyama choma, mishkaki, or ugali meal is complete without it.
longDesc: Pili pili is not one recipe — it is a category. Every Kenyan family makes it differently, every region has its own character, and every cook has their preferred balance of heat, acid, and aromatics. This is the classic all-purpose version — bright, fiery, and deeply flavoured. Adjust the chilli quantity for your preferred heat level.
ingredients: 8—12 fresh red or green chillies — adjust to heat preference

substitutions.alternative: Dried bird's eye chillies (use 4—6) for more concentrated heat
White vinegar for a sharper, more preserving version

equipment: Small saucepan — optional for cooked version
steps: Raw version: combine all ingredients in a blender. Pulse until roughly blended — some texture is desirable.
Taste and adjust salt and lemon. Serve immediately or refrigerate.
Cooked version (longer shelf life): blend all ingredients. Heat oil in a small saucepan over medium heat. Add blended mixture. Simmer for 5—8 minutes until slightly darkened. Cool before storing.
chefTips: Do not over-blend — pili pili should have some texture, not be a smooth puree.
The cooked version lasts longer in the refrigerator (up to 2 weeks) and develops a richer, slightly smoky flavour.
Taste before adding all the chillies — chilli heat varies enormously between varieties and seasons.
A pinch of sugar balances the heat without being detectable.
commonMistakes: Over-blending to a smooth puree — loses texture and visual appeal.
Under-salting — salt amplifies all the other flavours.

faqs.q: How do I control the heat level?
faqs.a: The seeds and white membrane of chillies contain most of the capsaicin. Remove them for milder pili pili; keep them for maximum heat. Start with fewer chillies — you can always add more.

cookingScience: Capsaicin (the heat compound in chillies) is fat-soluble — frying the blended pili pili in oil extracts and concentrates the capsaicin, making the cooked version more intensely hot than the same amount of raw chillies in the blended version.
sustainabilityTips: Grow chillies at home — they are among the most productive and easy garden plants.
storage: Raw version: refrigerate 5 days. Cooked version: refrigerate 2 weeks. Freeze both for 3 months.
reheating: Not required — serve at room temperature or cold.
healthBenefits: Chillies are rich in vitamin C.
culturalNote: Pili pili is as fundamental to Kenyan dining as ugali or chai — the condiment that gives every meal its finishing heat and character. No Kenyan table is properly set without it.
regionalVariations: Fresh pili pili — raw blended version.
Cooked pili pili — fried and cooked for longer life.
Coastal pili pili — with coconut milk added.
Dry pili pili — dried chillies only, no tomato.
Pili pili ya limau — extra lemon.
